section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: According to the passage, which of the following most directly explains why Spain's colonial wealth failed to produce domestic economic growth?

stimulus.image_caption: The silver mines of Potosi, woodcut from Cieza de Leon's Cronica del Peru, 1553.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Woodcut of Potosi from Pedro Cieza de Leon, Cronica del Peru, 1553; pre-1930
stimulus.text_stimulus: The flood of gold and silver pulled from mines in Mexico and the Andes by coerced labor was a fortune Spain might have used to modernize its farms, workshops, and trade networks — to close the gap with the more advanced economies of northwestern Europe. Instead, Spain stayed in the grip of a small ruling elite of crown, clergy, and great landowners. In Castile, two or three percent of the people held ninety-seven percent of the land, and those great proprietors saw no reason to change: they preferred to run ever-larger flocks of sheep and ship the raw wool to the Netherlands for finishing. Meanwhile the crown poured the American windfall into the largest standing army in Europe, touching off an arms race and a string of hegemonic wars against France, the Dutch, and England. The deepest effect of all that circulating silver was a prolonged inflation that rippled across Western Europe. — adapted from A. Kent MacDougall's account of sixteenth-century Spain

options: (A) American colonial governments kept nearly all colonial revenue through local taxation, sending little of it back to the crown.
(B) The crown poured the windfall into Europe's largest standing army and a string of hegemonic wars, while a small elite hoarded land and shipped raw wool abroad rather than investing at home.
(C) Dutch and English naval blockades cut Spain off from the trade networks it needed to commercialize its colonial wealth.
(D) The silver mines of Mexico and the Andes were largely exhausted within a generation, cutting off the flow of bullion to Spain.

section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

questions.stimulus_text: Historian Lynn Dumenil describes the 1920s as a decade when 'modernity collided with tradition' — new consumer goods, new freedoms for women, and new mass media unsettling older Protestant, small-town certainties.
parts: A. Briefly explain ONE example of social or cultural change in the 1920s.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of that change.
C. Briefly explain ONE example of resistance to social or cultural change in the 1920s.
exemplar: Mass consumer culture arrived: radios, refrigerators, and automobiles bought on installment plans, sold by a new advertising industry, reshaped daily life.
Women claimed new freedoms — the flapper, the vote (1920), and public figures from Dorothy Parker to Aimee Semple McPherson embodying female voices in literature and religion.
Resistance was fierce: Prohibition, the Scopes trial over evolution, the reborn Ku Klux Klan, and the 1924 immigration quotas defended a 'traditional' America against the new culture.

questions.stimulus_text: I discovered many islands inhabited by numerous people. I took possession of all of them for our most fortunate King... They are very fertile, and will be very useful.
questions.attribution: Christopher Columbus, letter to Luis de Santangel, February 1493 (contemporary translation).
parts: A. Briefly describe Columbus's claim about the lands he encountered, as expressed in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE motive that led the Spanish monarchs to sponsor Columbus's voyage.
C. Briefly explain ONE criticism of Spanish colonization that emerged in the decades after Columbus's voyages.
exemplar: Columbus claims the islands he reached for Spain are populous and valuable, and that by taking possession of them he has extended the Spanish crown's dominion across the ocean.
The Spanish monarchs funded Columbus because they sought direct access to the wealth of Asia - gold, spices, and trade routes that bypassed Portuguese and Ottoman middlemen.

Las Casas and other critics condemned the encomienda system and the violence of conquest, arguing that Spanish treatment of Native peoples violated Christian and natural law - the core of the Black Legend debate.

questions.stimulus_text: The photograph shows an enormous, densely packed crowd stretching from the Lincoln Memorial toward the Washington Monument - men, women, and children of many races, many holding signs demanding jobs and freedom. The demonstration is orderly and peaceful despite its vast size.
questions.attribution: Described from the 1963 photograph of the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom (National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons).
parts: A. Briefly describe what the photograph shows about the character of the 1963 March on Washington.
B. Briefly explain ONE effect the march had on federal policy.
C. Briefly explain ONE criticism of the march or of its achievements.
exemplar: The photograph captures the peaceful, massive scale of the demonstration - ordinary people filling the capital's public space - which signaled that the movement spoke for the nation, not a fringe.
The march pressured the federal government: within a year Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, outlawing segregation in public places and employment discrimination.

Critics argued the march's orderliness muted its radicalism - Malcolm X dismissed it as the 'Farce on Washington' - and that legislation alone did not end de facto segregation in housing, schools, or jobs.

section_2a.directions: Section II, Part A — Document-Based Question: 1 question, 60 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period). The question is based on 7 documents. In your response you must develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, use at least 4 documents to support your argument, use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents, and for at least 2 documents explain how the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to your argument. This part counts for 25 percent of the exam score.

dbq.prompt: Analyze the effects of American foreign policy in Latin America during the period 1899–1917.

documents.text: "Article III. The Government of Cuba consents that the United States may exercise the right to intervene for the preservation of Cuban independence, the maintenance of a government adequate for the protection of life property, and individual liberty, and for discharging the obligations with respect to Cuba imposed by the Treaty of Paris on the United States…" —Platt Amendment (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: A U.S. congressional amendment imposed on Cuba as a condition of American withdrawal; its purpose is to legalize future U.S. intervention. Argument relevance: Use to argue U.S. policy converted Cuban 'independence' into a protectorate—sovereignty limited by American veto power.

documents.text: "The Republic of Panama grants to the United States in perpetuity, the use, occupation and control of a zone of land … for the construction … of said canal. … The Republic of Panama further grants to the United States in perpetuity … any other lands and waters outside the zone … necessary and convenient for the construction … and protection of the said Canal." —Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: A treaty signed by the U.S. and a French agent days after Panama's U.S.-backed secession from Colombia; its purpose is to secure canal rights on American terms. Argument relevance: Use to argue U.S. policy manufactured a compliant client state to obtain the canal zone—intervention by treaty rather than troops.

documents.text: "Chronic wrongdoing, or an impotence which results in a general loosening of the ties of civilized society, may … ultimately require intervention by some civilized nation, and in the Western Hemisphere the adherence of the United States to the Monroe Doctrine may lead the United States, … in flagrant cases of such wrongdoing or impotence, to exercise an international police power." —Theodore Roosevelt, Annual Message to Congress (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Roosevelt announces his corollary to Congress as national policy; his purpose is to justify preemptive U.S. intervention in the Caribbean and Central America. Argument relevance: Use as the doctrinal centerpiece: the U.S. claimed a unilateral right to police the hemisphere, the ideological engine of the era's interventions.

documents.date: Produced for this item (replaces Harper's Weekly cartoon, 1907)
documents.text: An original illustration in the style of an early-1900s magazine cartoon: Uncle Sam sits at a banquet table piled with dishes labeled 'Cuba,' 'Puerto Rico,' 'Panama,' and 'Nicaragua,' while a figure labeled 'U.S. investor' carves the roast and waiters labeled 'U.S. Marines' stand ready. The caption reads 'The Full Dinner Pail,' suggesting that American prosperity was fed by economic dominance over Latin America.
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: A generated-original cartoon in the idiom of 1900s political satire; its purpose is to show how contemporaries could view U.S. policy as self-serving feasting. Argument relevance: Use to argue American policy served U.S. business interests first—pairs with Doc E (dollar diplomacy) and Doc F (anti-imperialist critique).
documents.caption: The Full Dinner Pail (generated-original cartoon in 1900s idiom)
documents.pd_rationale: generated-original: drawn by committed script make_dbq_svgs.py

documents.text: "The diplomacy of the present administration has sought to respond to modern ideas of commercial intercourse. This policy has been characterized by substituting dollars for bullets. … It is an effort frankly directed to the increase of American trade …" —William Howard Taft, Fourth Annual Message to Congress (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Taft defends his administration's record to Congress; his purpose is to present dollar diplomacy as peaceful, modern statecraft. Argument relevance: Use to argue U.S. policy tied Latin American economies to American banks and trade—economic leverage as the instrument of control.

documents.text: "It is proposed that in the Honduras and Nicaragua … the United States government should be authorized to secure the collection and disbursement of the revenue in the interest of American capitalists who contemplate making loans to those countries. This involves serious risk of complications which may lead to further interferences and ultimate control. … [We] recognize generally their independent right to govern (or misgovern) their own countries." —Erving Winslow, "Aggression in South America," Report of the Thirteen (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: An anti-imperialist activist warns the American public; his purpose is to expose how 'protecting' American loans becomes a pretext for controlling Latin American governments. Argument relevance: Use as the critical counter-voice: even contemporaries argued dollar diplomacy eroded Latin American sovereignty and invited endless intervention.

documents.text: "A series of incidents have recently occurred which cannot but create the impression that the representatives of General Huerta were willing to go out of their way to show disregard for the dignity and rights of this government … I, therefore, come to ask your approval that I should use the armed forces of the United States … as may be necessary to obtain from General Huerta … the fullest recognition of the rights and dignity of the United States…" —Woodrow Wilson, Address to Congress (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Wilson asks Congress to authorize force after the Tampico incident; his purpose is to justify occupying Veracruz and pressuring Huerta's regime. Argument relevance: Use to argue that even the 'moral diplomacy' president used military intervention in Mexico—showing continuity of interventionism across administrations.

section_2b.directions: Section II, Part B — Long Essay: 1 question, 40 minutes. Develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, and support your argument with specific and relevant examples. This part counts for 15 percent of the exam score. Total exam time: 3 hours 15 minutes.

leq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which differing ideas about the nature of government shaped the emergence of political parties in the 1780s and 1790s.
leq.guidance: Thesis frame: argue how Hamiltonian and Jeffersonian visions of government produced the first party system. Evidence buckets: Hamilton's financial program vs. Jeffersonian strict construction; the Bank and assumption debates; foreign-policy splits (Britain vs. France); the election of 1800 as the parties' first transfer of power.
